auction.scope: Google's quality-weighted second-price search auction as deployed 2002-2008 (AdWords Select), compared against pure-bid ranking (GoTo/Overture) and first-price with equilibrium bid shading, with a coda on the DOJ-disclosed pricing knobs that overrode the mechanism from 2019.

rigor.empirical_vs_illustrative: Every real-world number carries a calibration object under an 'evidence' entry. Every invented number sits inside an object marked illustrative:true and carries no calibration.

mechanism.name: AdWords Select: quality-weighted generalized second-price, self-serve, no minimums
mechanism.one_line: Rank by bid x predicted click-through rate; charge the minimum needed to hold position, quality-adjusted; let anyone in for five dollars.

formal.name: Quality-weighted generalized second-price (AdWords Select, deployed 2002-2008)
formal.players: Advertisers bidding a maximum CPC; Google, which also estimates the quality weight, validates the click and bills the log; searchers.
formal.strategies: Choose a max CPC per keyword. Bids and quality scores are private. From 2004 a bid-management industry (iProspect, Did-It, Performics, Efficient Frontier) sold strategy as a service.
formal.allocation_rule: AdRank = bid x predicted click-through rate. Sort by AdRank, descending. This is a ranking by expected revenue per impression, not by willingness to pay.
formal.payment_rule: Winner in slot j pays the minimum needed to hold position, quality-adjusted: p_j = (b_(j+1) * q_(j+1)) / q_j + $0.01, charged per click, capped at its own max CPC. The last slot pays the reserve.
formal.information: Bids private; the quality weight is computed by the seller and not disclosed as a number; the click count is produced and validated by the seller. No independent click-measurement standard existed until 2009.
formal.entry: One-time $5 activation fee, no minimum monthly spend, automated approval, most ads live immediately. (The era-6 record flags the widely-repeated 5-cent minimum bid as unsupported by its cited sources; Google's own 10-K example shows a $0.01 minimum.)
formal.objective_maximised: Expected revenue per impression, subject to the second-price discount.
deployed_divergences_from_textbook_gsp: The one-cent increment: prices are next-AdRank plus a fixed increment, not exactly next-AdRank.

From August 2005, a per-keyword dynamic minimum bid derived from Quality Score. This is a second, independent quality channel that acts as a PRICE, not a ranking weight, and it is the seller's number. See break-2.
Smart pricing (2004) discounted syndicated network clicks by expected value, so the same bid bought differently-priced clicks depending on where the ad ran.
Landing-page quality was folded into Quality Score in 2005, which is an admission that click-through rate alone rewards the wrong ad.

calibration.statement: AdWords Select, launched 20 February 2002, ranked ads by 'a combination of ad performance (click-thru rate) and how much an advertiser agrees to pay per click' and applied a discounter so advertisers 'pay the lowest amount possible' - quality-weighted second-price pricing from launch.
calibration.unit: year (2002-02-20), launch of the quality-weighted CPC auction

sources.name: Google press release, 'Google Introduces New Pricing For Popular Self-Service Online Advertising Program' (Feb 20, 2002)

calibration.statement: Google's own AdWords Discounter example: maximum bids of $1.00, $0.60 and $0.50 per click produce prices of $0.61, $0.51 and $0.01 (the minimum bid) - the winner pays one cent above the next bid, not its own bid, and the last slot pays the seller's reserve.
calibration.unit: USD paid per click by the top advertiser bidding $1.00 against a $0.60 next bid

mechanism.what_is_allocated: Ranked ad slots against a query, per impression. Payment is per click, so the seller bears the click risk and the estimate of click probability is the seller's.
mechanism.the_reframe: AdRank is not a relevance filter with a revenue side effect. It is a ranking by expected revenue per impression, which happens to reward relevance because clicks are the shared currency of both parties. Every result in this analysis follows from that one substitution: the auction sells impressions and prices clicks.

baselines.counterfactual_note: Where a claim needs a no-mechanism baseline rather than a rival, the baseline used is Overture's deployed pure-bid auction as it actually ran in 2002 (10-cent floor, $20 monthly minimum, human editorial review, $0.31 realised average CPC), not an idealised pure-bid design.

pure_bid.name: Pure-bid ranking, pay-per-click (GoTo/Overture, 1998-2007)
pure_bid.players: Advertisers bidding a maximum cost-per-click on a keyword; a search engine allocating ranked listing slots; searchers.
pure_bid.strategies: Choose a max CPC per keyword. Bids were publicly visible in Overture's bid tool, which made bid wars observable and gap strategies routine.
pure_bid.allocation_rule: Sort by bid alone, descending. Highest bid takes the top slot.
pure_bid.payment_rule: Winner in slot j pays the bid of the advertiser in slot j+1, plus one cent. Charged per click.
pure_bid.information: Bids public. Human editorial review of every listing.
pure_bid.entry: 10-cent minimum bid per listing, $20 minimum monthly spend, human editorial approval.
pure_bid.objective_maximised: Willingness to pay per CLICK. The seller's revenue per IMPRESSION is whatever falls out.
pure_bid.deployed_notes: Overture's realised average price per click was $0.31 in 2002. It was the paid-search revenue leader that year ($667.7m against Google's $439.5m of total revenue), so the design was commercially viable, not broken. Yahoo replaced it with quality weighting (Panama) only on 5 February 2007.

calibration.statement: Overture's pure-bid auction ranked listings by bid alone and gated entry: all new US advertisers had to commit to a minimum bid of 10 cents per listing and a $20 minimum monthly spend, with human editorial review of every listing. Its realised average price per paid click was $0.31 in 2002, up from $0.20 in 2001.
calibration.unit: USD average realised price per paid introduction (click), Overture FY2002

sources.name: Overture Services, Inc., Form 10-K FY2002

calibration.statement: The pure-bid auction was not failing commercially when the quality-weighted auction arrived: Overture booked $667.7m of revenue in 2002 against Google's $439.5m of total revenue, and was the paid-search revenue leader entering the era.
calibration.unit: USD millions, Overture revenue FY2002

sources.name: Overture Services, Inc., Form 10-K FY2002

first_price_shading.name: Unified first-price auction with equilibrium bid shading (Google Ad Manager display exchange, from 2019-09-05)
first_price_shading.players: Demand-side platforms and exchanges bidding on behalf of advertisers; publishers setting unified pricing rules; Google operating both the exchange and the publisher ad server.
first_price_shading.strategies: Bid a shaded value: b(v) = v * (n-1)/n in the symmetric benchmark, or in practice the output of a proprietary bid-shading model estimating the clearing price.
first_price_shading.allocation_rule: Highest bid wins (quality-weighted equivalents apply where a quality term exists).
first_price_shading.information: The clearing price is set by the buyer's own model rather than by the runner-up's bid. Google committed to bid data files for publishers and post-auction feedback for buyers as part of the change.
first_price_shading.objective_maximised: Nothing new. Under symmetry, IPV and risk neutrality this is revenue-equivalent to second price for every n - see ex-4.
first_price_shading.why_it_happened: Header bidding (2014-15, standardised by Prebid.js) made publishers compare a first-price header bid against a second-price exchange result run by their own ad server. First price plus unified pricing rules made the comparison apples-to-apples. Google's own stated finding was that first-price auctions have a 'neutral to positive impact on a publisher's total revenue' - a transparency and competitive-pressure change, not a yield change.
first_price_shading.scope_warning: THIS WAS DISPLAY, NOT SEARCH. Google Search never moved to first price. The 2019 search-side change was rGSP, which the DOJ record shows was an explicit revenue play. Conflating the two is the standard error in retellings of the 2019 transition.

calibration.statement: Google Ad Manager - the open-web DISPLAY exchange, not search - completed its move to a unified first-price auction from 5 September 2019, folding publisher floors into unified pricing rules. Google's stated rationale was a fair and transparent marketplace under header-bidding competition, and it reported that testing showed first-price auctions have a 'neutral to positive impact on a publisher's total revenue'.
calibration.unit: year (2019-09-05), Google Ad Manager unified first-price rollout

sources.name: Google Ad Manager blog, 'Rolling out first price auctions to Google Ad Manager partners' (Sep 5, 2019)
Google Ad Manager blog, 'Simplifying programmatic: first price auctions for Google Ad Manager' (Mar 2019)

calibration.statement: Google's rGSP (randomized generalized second-price) auction, launched on SEARCH in 2019, raised top-slot cost-per-click on non-navigational queries by 5.91% on PCs and tablets and 4.85% on mobile in pre-launch experiments, with a 40-50% long-term stickage factor; a 5.74% revenue gain persisted two months after launch. Advertisers cannot opt out.
calibration.unit: percent increase in top-slot CPC on PC/tablet from rGSP

sources.name: United States v. Google LLC, Mem. Op., No. 20-cv-3010 (APM), Doc. 1033 (D.D.C. Aug. 5, 2024), FOF paras 245-255

vcg_benchmark.name: Vickrey-Clarke-Groves position auction (truthful benchmark, never deployed on search)
vcg_benchmark.allocation_rule: Same efficient allocation as quality-weighted GSP: sort by bid x quality.
vcg_benchmark.payment_rule: Each winner pays the externality it imposes on the others: the sum over lower positions of (click difference) x (displaced bidder's value).
vcg_benchmark.property: Truthful bidding is a dominant strategy, so the mechanism's revenue is a determinate number rather than a band.
vcg_benchmark.why_it_matters_here: VCG is the yardstick that turns 'GSP is not truthful' from an adjective into arithmetic. In ex-2/ex-3 VCG revenue is $440, exactly the lowest locally-envy-free GSP equilibrium; naive truthful play under GSP yields $760. The difference between those two numbers is the value of advertiser sophistication, and it is 73% of the floor.

calibration.statement: The pure-bid auction was not failing commercially when the quality-weighted auction arrived: Overture booked $667.7m of revenue in 2002 against Google's $439.5m of total revenue, and was the paid-search revenue leader entering the era.
calibration.unit: USD millions, Overture revenue FY2002

sources.name: Overture Services, Inc., Form 10-K FY2002
Google Inc., Form 10-K FY2004 (2002 revenue table)

gsp_not_truthful.summary: With slot click volumes of 100 and 80 and values of $10, $6 and $2, the top bidder earns $400 by bidding its value and $640 by bidding $5. The deviation survives the one-cent increment ($399 vs $639.20) and survives quality weighting, because a common quality divisor rescales both sides of the comparison equally. GSP's payment rule ties your price to the bid below you, so buying a worse slot buys a cheaper price - the exact trade VCG closes and GSP leaves open.
gsp_not_truthful.consequence_for_the_other_claims: GSP revenue is a band, not a number: [$440 lowest locally-envy-free equilibrium = VCG revenue, $760 naive truthful play], a 1.727x spread. Claims C2 and C3 are proven at equal bids; the equilibrium correction runs in the advertisers' favour, and any simulator that shows truthful bidding overstates GSP revenue by up to 73%.

rgsp_coda.verdict: DEMONSTRATED for all three knobs; squashing's exponent is assumed because it has never been disclosed.
rgsp_coda.thesis: By 2019 the mechanism was no longer doing the pricing. Three named knobs were, and each one moves price with quality, allocation and creative held fixed.

knobs.what_it_does: Ranks and prices on b * q^gamma with gamma < 1, compressing the quality dimension so the winner's price rises toward the runner-up's raw bid.
knobs.worked_result: Markup = (q_next/q_own)^(gamma-1). At gamma = 0.95026 on a 0.03/0.08 quality gap the markup is exactly +5%, matching Dischler's disclosed average. At gamma = 0.5 on the ex-1 cast it restores the PURE-BID ranking - 18 clicks per 1000 impressions instead of 58 - while collecting 45.3% more total revenue than pure-bid ever did for that same worse allocation.
knobs.parameter_status: assumed - not in the public record

knobs.what_it_does: Applies a separate price multiplier to ad formats. No ranking change.
knobs.worked_result: A 20% share of observed RPM implies a 25% uplift on the counterfactual base; at the disclosed +15% per launch with about half retained, three launches compound to +24.2%, so the disclosed share is roughly three launches deep. At 2008 revenue levels a 20% RPM knob is worth $4,226m - 42% of the entire US newspaper classified market that year.
knobs.parameter_status: disclosed in the Mehta findings of fact

knobs.what_it_does: Randomises the ordering of similarly-scored ads so a lower-Ad-Rank ad can appear above a higher one, breaking the reliability of the bid-down-a-slot trade that makes shading profitable under plain GSP. Advertisers cannot opt out.
knobs.worked_result: Disclosed +5.91% top-slot CPC on PC/tablet and +4.85% on mobile in pre-launch tests, 40-50% stickage, +5.74% revenue persisting two months post-launch. Placed against the ex-3 equilibrium band, +5.74% traverses only 7.9% of the distance from the lowest equilibrium to naive truthful play. The knob did not have to be big, because GSP's own band is 73% wide and the seller sits on it.
knobs.parameter_status: magnitudes disclosed; the pricing rule itself is not public

rgsp_coda.continuity_finding: The knobs are not a break with the 2002-2008 mechanism. The reserve-price channel was already a direct seller-set price from August 2005 (quality-based minimum bids), and on a one-bidder query the reserve IS the price - see break-2, where moving the minimum bid from $0.01 to $1.00 changes revenue 100x with one advertiser, one ad and one user experience. What 2019 added was scale and a trial transcript.
rgsp_coda.open_tension: The record says rGSP replaced format pricing because rGSP made more money, yet format pricing was ~20% of text-ads RPM while rGSP's disclosed persistent revenue effect was +5.74%. Either the 20% was not all incremental, or the two knobs were substitutes extracting the same surplus. The record as summarised does not resolve this and this analysis does not assert a resolution.

examples.claim: C1 + C2 + C3: pure-bid ranking places lower-revenue ads above higher-revenue ads once clickthrough differs enough; quality-weighting raises TOTAL revenue and relevance together; and under GSP every winner pays less than its bid while total revenue still exceeds the pure-bid outcome.

assumptions: Predicted CTR equals true CTR (relaxed in break-1).

Position multipliers are separable from advertiser quality: expected clicks = impressions x position_multiplier x advertiser_ctr. This is the standard separable position-auction assumption and is what Google's own ranking arithmetic implies.
Bids are held fixed across designs so the ranking and pricing rules are the only thing that changes. Equilibrium bid response is handled separately in ex-2 and ex-3.

setup.structure: 2 slots, 3 bidders, equal quality (q = 1 for all, so quality-weighting is neutral and only the payment rule is under test).
assumptions: Complete information, as in the standard textbook treatment (Edelman-Ostrovsky-Schwarz 2007; Varian 2007).
Increment set to zero in the headline arithmetic; the one-cent version is computed to show it changes nothing.
Setting q = 1 is deliberate: quality-weighting does not restore truthfulness, because dividing every bid and price by a fixed quality term leaves the deviation's sign unchanged.

The deviation survives the one-cent increment ($399 vs $639.20) and survives quality-weighting, because a common quality divisor rescales both sides equally. GSP is a second-price auction only in its arithmetic, not in its incentives: the price a winner pays is set by the bid below it, so buying a lower slot buys a lower price, and that is exactly the trade GSP leaves open and VCG closes.

examples.claim: C4 corollary: because GSP is not truthful, its revenue is not a number but a band. The naive-truthful figure a simulator would display is the ceiling, not the equilibrium.

setup.structure: Same cast and slots as ex-2. We compute the LOWEST symmetric / locally-envy-free equilibrium of GSP using the standard recursion alpha_j * p_j = alpha_(j+1) * p_(j+1) + (alpha_j - alpha_(j+1)) * v_(j+1).
assumptions: Varian (2007) symmetric Nash equilibrium / Edelman-Ostrovsky-Schwarz (2007) locally envy-free equilibrium. The equilibria form a lattice; the lowest one is revenue-equivalent to VCG, and any locally envy-free equilibrium yields at least VCG revenue.

equilibrium check: Vale's payoff if it dropped to slot 2 - lower, so Vale stays
the GSP revenue band is 1.727x wide: $440 at the bottom equilibrium, $760 at naive truthful play

examples.conclusion: BOUNDED, and this is the single most important caveat on C2 and C3. GSP revenue in this example is anywhere in [$440, $760] depending on how well bidders play - a 73% band. Naive advertisers who bid their value hand the seller the top of the band; sophisticated ones (or the bid-management shops that grew up in this era) push toward the bottom. Any comparison of GSP against pure-bid that holds bids fixed - including ex-1 - therefore measures the mechanism at a point the bidders choose, not at a point the mechanism determines. The honest statement of C2/C3 is 'at equal bids', and the equilibrium correction runs in the advertisers' favour.

examples.claim: C5: first-price with rational bid shading converges to the same expected revenue as second-price - exactly, for every number of bidders, in the symmetric benchmark.

setup.structure: One slot. n bidders, values drawn independently and uniformly on [$0, $10]. Second-price/GSP: truthful bidding is dominant, revenue = the second-highest value. First-price: the symmetric equilibrium bid is b(v) = v*(n-1)/n, revenue = the winning bid.
setup.order_statistics: For n iid uniform draws on [0, V], E[k-th highest] = V*(n+1-k)/(n+1). So E[max] = V*n/(n+1) and E[2nd] = V*(n-1)/(n+1).
assumptions: Independent private values, symmetric bidders, risk neutrality, no reserve. These are exactly the conditions of the revenue-equivalence theorem, and each one is a place the result can break - see break-3.
One slot rather than two, so the arithmetic is closed-form. The position-auction version has the same qualitative answer via the equilibrium band in ex-3.

n=3: first-price expected revenue at shading factor 2/3

n=5: first-price expected revenue at shading factor 4/5
n=10: second-price expected revenue
n=10: first-price expected revenue at shading factor 9/10
the difference is exactly zero
SENSITIVITY: if the market over-shades to 0.60 instead of 0.6667 (n=3)
the seller loses 10% - revenue is linear in the shading factor
if the market under-shades to 0.7333
the seller gains 10%
THE NAIVE ERROR: Google's own 10-K example, total collected under the discounter
the same bids under pay-your-bid, if nobody re-bid
which looks like an 86% revenue windfall for first price
and is entirely an artefact of holding bids fixed: shading each bidder down to what it paid under the discounter returns the seller to $1.13

examples.conclusion: C5 PROVEN in the benchmark and BOUNDED outside it. First-price revenue with equilibrium shading equals second-price revenue exactly, for n = 2, 3, 5 and 10 - the algebra collapses to V*(n-1)/(n+1) in both cases. The switch is therefore not a yield mechanism. What the switch does move is who computes the price: under second-price the seller's runner-up sets it, under first-price the buyer's shading model sets it, which is why the 2019 change was fought over on transparency grounds. The seller's exposure is linear in the market's average shading factor: a market shading 10% too hard pays the seller 10% less.

examples.claim: BREAK on C5: revenue equivalence is a theorem about a benchmark, and the deployed display market violated three of its conditions.

conditions_and_violations: SYMMETRY. Buyers had asymmetric data and asymmetric shading models. Under first price the better shader wins more often at a lower price; under second price the price is set by the runner-up regardless of who shades better. Asymmetry breaks revenue equivalence in both directions and its sign is an empirical question, not a theorem.

AN HONEST SECOND PRICE. Header bidding (2014-15) put the exchange's second-price result in direct comparison with first-price header bids, and the exchange operator was also the publisher's ad server. If the party computing the second price also intermediates the auction, 'second price' is not observable to the publisher; a first price is.

A FIXED RESERVE. Unified pricing rules changed floors at the same time as the pricing rule, so the 2019 change was two changes at once and the pricing-rule effect cannot be isolated from the floor effect in publisher revenue data.
assumptions: Illustrative sensitivity only; no calibrated estimate of the 2019 revenue effect is asserted here beyond Google's own reported 'neutral to positive' finding.

steps.note: at equilibrium shading the ratio is exactly 1.00
a market shading at 0.55 hands the seller 17.5% less than second price
a market shading at 0.80 hands the seller 20% more
so the whole revenue question sits inside a 37.5-point spread in one behavioural parameter the seller does not control

examples.conclusion: BOUNDED. C5's 'converges toward similar expected revenue' holds exactly under symmetry, IPV, risk neutrality and a common reserve, and is otherwise a claim about where the market's shading models happen to sit. The defensible version of C5 is the negative one, and it is strong: nothing in the first-price rule mechanically raises yield, so a yield-magic explanation of 2019 has no mechanism behind it, while the transparency and header-bidding explanations have both a documented motive and Google's own 'neutral to positive' revenue finding.

examples.claim: C6a: squashing raises the price with the allocation, the ad copy and the user experience held constant - and at a heavy setting it also destroys the relevance gain that justified quality-weighting in the first place.

setup.rule: Rank by b * q^gamma instead of b * q, and price the winner at the runner-up's squashed score divided by the winner's own squashed quality: p = b_next * (q_next/q_own)^gamma. gamma = 1 is textbook AdRank. gamma < 1 compresses the quality dimension, which raises the winner's price toward the runner-up's raw bid whenever the winner is the higher-quality ad.

assumptions: gamma is an ASSUMED parameter. Squashing is named in the DOJ findings of fact; its exponent has never been disclosed. gamma = 0.5 is used to make the mechanism legible, and a gamma calibrated to the disclosed ~5% price effect is computed alongside it.
Prices are capped at the advertiser's own max CPC, as in the deployed product. No cap binds in either part.

At gamma = 0.95026 it raises the winner's price by exactly the ~5% Google's ads VP described, on an unchanged allocation. At gamma = 0.5 it does something sharper: on the ex-1 cast it restores the PURE-BID ranking - 18 clicks instead of 58 - while collecting 45.3% more revenue than pure-bid ever did for that same worse allocation. That is the cleanest available statement of the coda's thesis: the knob raises price and lowers relevance, moving opposite to the 2002 design on both metrics at once.

'About half' of the 15% is taken as exactly 50%, matching the 40-50% stickage band disclosed for rGSP.

examples.claim: C6c: rGSP does not need to break the auction to move the price. GSP's own equilibrium band is 73% wide, and the disclosed rGSP effect is a small move inside a band the seller controls the shape of.

setup.disclosed: rGSP launched on search in 2019; pre-launch experiments raised top-slot CPC by 5.91% on PC/tablet and 4.85% on mobile, with a 40-50% long-term stickage factor, and a 5.74% revenue gain persisted two months after launch. Advertisers cannot opt out.
setup.mechanism_note: rGSP randomises the ordering of similarly-scored ads, so a lower-Ad-Rank ad can appear above a higher one. The rationale in the record is revenue. Its effect on incentives is to break the reliability of the bid-down-a-slot trade that ex-2 shows is profitable under plain GSP, which pushes equilibrium play up off the ex-3 floor. The exact pricing rule is NOT public; this analysis therefore locates the disclosed magnitudes inside the ex-3 band rather than re-deriving them.
assumptions: The ex-3 band ($440 lowest equilibrium, $760 naive truthful) is an illustrative example, not a measurement of Google's book. The mapping is a scale illustration of how little the knob has to move.
Top-slot CPC and total revenue are different metrics measured over different windows; they are reported separately here rather than reconciled.

The mechanism did not have to be replaced to become a price-setting instrument. It only had to be tuned, and the tuning was undisclosed.

breaks.statement: The revenue and relevance case for quality-weighting is a bet on a click-through estimate produced by the party that collects the money, with no third-party audit standard until 2009.
breaks.worked: break-1-ctr-misestimation: if Cedar's true CTR is below 1.99% against a predicted 5%, quality-weighting earns LESS than pure-bid. Break-even overstatement is 2.52x.
breaks.who_it_favours: the seller, because the seller both sets and verifies the parameter

breaks.statement: Bidding below value strictly dominates truthful bidding for the top bidder. Revenue is a 1.727x band, not a number.
breaks.who_it_favours: sophisticated advertisers - which is why the 2002-2008 era grew a bid-management industry rather than a copywriting one

breaks.statement: b x q maximises expected revenue per impression. Relevance improves only insofar as clicks proxy relevance, and click-through rate alone rewards whatever gets clicked, including ads that mislead. Google's own remedy - folding landing-page quality into Quality Score in 2005 - is the admission.
breaks.worked: ex-1 shows the co-movement; the 2005 Quality Score change shows the seller did not trust CTR alone.
breaks.who_it_favours: high-CTR advertisers regardless of post-click value; corrected only by adding more seller-computed, undisclosed quality terms

breaks.statement: A second-price auction needs a second bidder. On a one-bidder query the price is the reserve, and from August 2005 the reserve was a per-keyword, per-advertiser, Quality-Score-derived number the seller computed and never published.
breaks.worked: break-2-reserve-is-a-posted-price: $0.01 vs $1.00 minimum bid is a 100x revenue change with one advertiser and no change to anything the user sees.
breaks.who_it_favours: the seller, unconditionally, on the majority of distinct queries

breaks.statement: Overture published bids in its bid tool. Visible bids make tacit collusion and gap-jumping easy: an advertiser can park one cent above a rival and watch for retaliation, and rivals can settle into a stable rotation without communicating. Google's move to private bids and a private quality term removed that surface - and replaced it with a different one, in which no bidder can audit the price it is charged.
breaks.worked: not separately computed; the design-level point is that both designs carry an information asymmetry, pointing in opposite directions.
breaks.who_it_favours: pure-bid: incumbent bidders who can watch each other. GSP: the seller.

breaks.statement: Revenue equivalence needs symmetry, IPV, risk neutrality and a common reserve. The 2019 display market violated symmetry (asymmetric shading models), had an interested party computing the second price (the exchange operator was also the ad server), and changed floors at the same time (unified pricing rules).
breaks.worked: break-3-revenue-equivalence-fails: seller revenue is linear in the market's shading factor, spanning -17.5% to +20% across a plausible 0.55-0.80 range.
breaks.who_it_favours: whichever side has the better clearing-price model - which under first price is the buyer, and that is the actual behavioural change of 2019

breaks.type: deployed variant diverges from the textbook rule
breaks.statement: The textbook GSP was overridden in production by squashing, format pricing and rGSP, none disclosed to advertisers, none opt-outable, all raising price without raising quality.
breaks.who_it_favours: the seller; and the continuity with the 2005 reserve channel means this is a difference of degree, not of kind

findings.text: Pure-bid ranking mis-orders by expected revenue exactly when 1 < b_i/b_j < q_j/q_i. In the worked case the bid ratio is 3 and the CTR ratio is 5, so the pure-bid order (Aster, Brindle, Cedar) is the precise reverse of the expected-revenue order.

Same example, both metrics: revenue per 1000 impressions rises from $28.18 to $52.58 (+86.6%) and clicks delivered rise from 18 to 58 (+222%). The two metrics move together because clicks are the currency of both sides.

The revenue gain is a VOLUME effect, not a price effect. Average price per click FALLS 42%, from $1.57 to $0.91. Pure-bid maximises willingness to pay per click; AdRank maximises revenue per impression, and impressions are the scarce good. Every retelling that describes quality-weighting as letting Google charge more has the sign backwards.

The gain survives only while the seller's click-through estimate is roughly right. At a predicted 5% against a true CTR under 1.99%, quality-weighting earns less than the crude design it replaced. No independent standard for counting a click existed until 2009 and no MRC accreditation of search click counting existed in period, so this parameter was unauditable throughout the era.

Both GSP winners pay below their bids ($0.81 against $1.00; $1.51 against $2.00) and the total is still 1.87x the pure-bid total. GSP collects 79.7% of what pay-your-bid would collect on the same bids and still beats pure-bid by 87%, because it is charging a smaller margin on a much larger click base.

GSP is not truthful: $400 truthful against $640 shaded, in a three-bidder two-slot example, robust to the one-cent increment and to quality weighting. Under VCG the same bidder earns $720 by telling the truth.

The consequence is that GSP revenue is a band of [$440, $760] - a factor of 1.727 - whose position depends on advertiser sophistication rather than on the mechanism. The lowest equilibrium is exactly VCG-revenue-equivalent. Any comparison holding bids fixed, including this analysis's own C1-C3 example, measures a point the bidders choose. A simulator that displays truthful bidding overstates GSP revenue by up to 73%.

First-price with equilibrium shading and second-price yield identical expected revenue for n = 2, 3, 5 and 10 - both collapse to V*(n-1)/(n+1). There is no yield mechanism in the first-price rule. The apparent 86% windfall from Google's own 10-K bid example ($2.10 versus $1.13) is entirely an artefact of freezing bids.

Equivalence needs symmetry, IPV, risk neutrality and a common reserve. Seller revenue is linear in the market's average shading factor, spanning -17.5% to +20% over a 0.55-0.80 range against an equilibrium 0.667. The 2019 change's real effect is that the clearing price moved from being computed by the seller's runner-up to being computed by the buyer's model - which is exactly the transparency argument, since the previous second-price computation was performed by a party that also intermediated the auction.

The two 2019 changes ran in opposite directions on opposite sides of the business: display went to unified first price on 2019-09-05 with a transparency rationale and a self-reported neutral-to-positive revenue effect, while search got rGSP with an explicit revenue rationale and a disclosed +5.74% persistent gain. Search never went first-price. This is the most common factual error in retellings of 2019 and the analysis must state it explicitly.

Each knob moves price with quality, allocation and creative held constant. Squashing at gamma = 0.95026 delivers exactly the +5% Dischler described on a 0.03/0.08 quality gap; at gamma = 0.5 on the era-6 cast it restores the pure-bid ranking (18 clicks instead of 58) while collecting 45.3% more than pure-bid. Format pricing's disclosed 20% RPM share is roughly three compounding launches of the disclosed size. rGSP's disclosed +5.74% traverses 7.9% of GSP's own equilibrium band.

The knobs did not have to be large, and they did not have to replace the auction. GSP already under-determined revenue by 73% because the payment depends on how well bidders play; the seller sits on that band and the knobs are instruments for moving the market inside it. The mechanism became a price-setting instrument by being tuned, not by being abandoned.

The pricing-knob story starts in era 6, not in 2019. From August 2005 Quality Score set per-keyword minimum bids, and on a one-bidder query the minimum bid IS the price - moving it from $0.01 to $1.00 is a 100x revenue change with one advertiser, one ad and no change to the user's experience. The seller has been setting prices directly on the long tail since three years before the era closed.

This analysis proves the design is better on the metric it optimises. It does not prove the design caused the capture. Overture ran the pure-bid auction and led paid-search revenue through 2002 ($667.7m against Google's $439.5m of total revenue); Yahoo adopted quality weighting only on 5 February 2007, five years late and long after the distribution war was settled. The auction explains yield per query; it does not explain query volume. Read this section against the distribution engine, not instead of it.
findings.decided_by: ex-1 plus the era-6 record (mech-overture-002, mech-panama-001)

findings.text: Every parameter that decides who wins and what they pay - predicted click-through rate, the quality-based reserve, the squashing exponent, the format multiplier, the click validity test - was computed by the seller, undisclosed as a number, and unaudited by any third party. That is the same institutional fact in 2005 and in 2019. The mechanism-design case for the auction is sound; the governance case never existed.
